summary: Defines the manifest, a signed list of every file at an RPKI publication point along with a hash of each. Receivers can use it to detect missing, altered or stale files. It was replaced by RFC 9286.

eli5.summary: A manifest is a signed packing slip listing every file in a folder and its fingerprint. It lets you notice if something has gone missing or been changed. It was later replaced by RFC 9286.

questions: how to detect missing rpki objects
subtitle: Signed file inventory to detect missing, altered, or stale objects in RPKI repositories.

tldr.problem: Digital signatures in RPKI protect against modification but not against deletion or replay of stale objects—an attacker can remove a revocation or substitute an old version without being detected.
tldr.mechanism: A manifest is a signed list of all files at a certification authority's repository point, with a hash and timestamp for each. Relying parties can check actual files against the manifest to detect missing, altered, or stale objects, and determine the manifest's own currency by comparing timestamps.
tldr.outcome: RPKI relying parties gain protection against object deletion and stale-object replay attacks, enabling secure routing validation. RFC 9286 later updated the format.

today: RFC 6486 defines manifests for RPKI and is used by relying parties to validate the integrity and completeness of RPKI repositories. The specification was updated by RFC 9286, which refines the manifest format and validation procedures. Manifests remain a critical component of the RPKI security model, enabling detection of attacks against the repository system itself.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) uses digital certificates and signed objects to enable secure routing. Every signed object is protected by cryptographic signatures verifying that no one modified it after publication. However, signatures do not protect against deletion (removing a revocation list or a stale certificate) or replay (publishing an old version of an object in place of a newer one).

A manifest addresses these gaps by providing a signed inventory. A manifest lists every signed object (certificate, CRL, ROA, etc.) that a certification authority publishes at a repository location, along with a hash of each file. If relying parties detect that the actual files do not match the manifest's list, they can identify missing objects or substituted stale versions and choose appropriate protective action.
sections.eli5: Signatures prove nobody changed a file. But signatures don't prove a file wasn't deleted or swapped for an older version. A manifest shows the complete list and fingerprints, so you can tell if files are missing or outdated.

sections.title: Manifest Structure and Scope
sections.content:
A manifest is an RPKI signed object (CMS SignedData structure) containing a manifest body with these fields:

  • version: must be 0.
  • manifestNumber: an integer incremented with each new manifest, allowing detection of missing updates.
  • thisUpdate and nextUpdate: GeneralizedTime values marking the manifest's validity period, modeled after X.509 CRL timestamps.
  • fileHashAlg: OID of the hash algorithm (SHA-256 or SHA-512 per RFC 6485).
  • fileList: sequence of filename and hash pairs for every published object at the CA's repository point.

The manifest itself is not included in the fileList (a circular dependency). For each CA instance publishing at the repository point, there is exactly one current manifest; multiple CA instances (during key rollover) may have separate manifests.
sections.eli5: A manifest says 'version 1', 'issued now, expires then', 'uses this fingerprint method', and then lists 'file1.cer has hash X, file2.crl has hash Y, ...'.

sections.title: Manifest Generation
sections.content:
When generating a manifest, the CA follows a procedure: optionally generate a new key pair; issue an EE (end-entity) certificate for signing (using either one-time-use or sequential-use mode); construct the manifest content listing all published objects and the most recent CRL; sign it with the EE certificate's private key; and publish it. The EE certificate itself is NOT published at the repository point (only embedded in the signed object wrapper).

The CA MUST issue a new manifest before the nextUpdate time and whenever the collection of published objects changes. If using one-time-use certificates, the private key is destroyed after signing. If using sequential-use certificates, the same key signs multiple manifests in sequence, and the EE certificate's validity must encompass all manifest validity periods.
sections.eli5: The authority makes a signed list of everything in the folder, including the hash of each file, and publishes that list. If the folder changes, a new list is published with an updated number.

sections.title: Relying Party Checks
sections.content:
To use a manifest safely, a relying party performs checks in order:

  • Select the current manifest (highest manifestNumber among valid manifests).
  • Verify that every file at the repository appears in one manifest and every manifest entry appears in the repository (completeness check).
  • Verify the current time falls between thisUpdate and nextUpdate (staleness check).
  • Hash every file at the repository and verify the hash matches the manifest (integrity check).
  • Verify the manifest conforms to scope constraints (e.g., entries are only for objects issued by that CA).

If all checks pass for a signed object and its full certification path, the RP can conclude that no deletion or replay attack has compromised that object. If checks fail, the RP applies local policy: a missing manifest, stale manifest, or hash mismatch triggers warnings and may prompt the RP to reject objects or use cached versions.
sections.eli5: Check that the list is current, that every file in the folder is listed, that every listed file exists, and that each file's fingerprint matches. If all match, nothing was deleted or swapped.

sections.title: Error Conditions and Recovery
sections.content:
The RFC defines several error states and recommended responses:

  • Missing manifest: No protection against deletion or replay; objects SHOULD be viewed as suspect and used only per local policy.
  • Invalid manifest: The manifest fails syntactic or semantic checks; MUST be discarded; use other valid manifests if available.
  • Stale manifest: Current time is past nextUpdate; objects SHOULD be treated as suspect; risk of undetected deletions or stale CRLs causing revoked certificates to be trusted.
  • Hash mismatch: A file's actual hash differs from the manifest; may indicate publisher error or attack; local policy determines use.
  • Mismatch between manifest and repository: Files missing from repository but listed in manifest indicate deletion; files in repository but not in manifest indicate publisher error or replay of stale manifest.

RPs should maintain local caches of recently seen valid manifests to use as fallback when current manifests are unavailable or suspect.
sections.eli5: If the list is missing, deleted, outdated, or the files don't match, the RP warns the operator and decides whether to trust the files anyway or reject them.
